Can AI make Thanksgiving less painful?

📅 25 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (885 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Mashable

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • I have a liberal friend who I was talking with the other day about looks for Thanksgiving.
  • Industry observers note that "I’m dreading it," he said.
  • Every November, we all pretend that turkey, stuffing, and pumpkin pie are worth being trapped by three generations of relatives you barely know.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

I have a liberal friend who I was talking with the other day about looks for Thanksgiving. He’s going home to his family in Oklahoma, who are anything but liberal.

Industry observers note that "I’m dreading it," he said. "My uncle sits in a chair watching Fox News on his phone, and my great-aunt will try to tell me in so many ways, without telling me, that I’m going to hell for being gay.".

Every November, we all pretend that turkey, stuffing, and pumpkin pie are worth being trapped by three generations of relatives you barely know. Just call me the Grinch of Thanksgiving.

Sources indicate that sure, not all of us are in an inhospitable environment like that, but for many, it's as awkward as waving back at someone on the street who was actually waving at the person behind you. When the atmosphere is heavy, with everyone waiting for the proverbial shoe to drop, it inevitably does — loudly, like a construction boot.

Years ago, with a former partner’s parents, the mother dropped her fork, pointed across the table at me, and stated in Spanish, "I can’t look at him." It was all downhill from there.

It has been revealed that back in the day, before technology swallowed us whole and gave us hunched necks, surviving Thanksgiving required biting your tongue, heavy drinking — though that often fueled the fires of ferocity — or staying away. Your only defenses were hiding in the bathroom, taking a long nap, or pretending to be a die-hard Detroit Lions fan (they traditionally play every Thanksgiving), eyes and ears glued to the TV to tune out the bickering.

Sources indicate that if you wanted to fact-check a wild political claim your uncle blurted out, you just had to let him win because you couldn’t pull the truth up on your phone. If you needed a sounding board before walking into the lion's den, you had to psych yourself up alone, and rehearse answers in your car at the end of the driveway.

This year, however, things look different. Lately, we’ve spent plenty of time worrying about how artificial intelligence is taking over the internet and creeping into our daily routines. It is everywhere now. There’s no arguing that fact with your uncle.

Yet one of its most underrated perks is acting as a real-time social buffer. AI has quietly become an infinitely patient wingman sitting right in your pocket, ready to keep your holiday civil, lighthearted, and blissfully brief on drama.

It has been revealed that think about the dread before you even walk through the front door. Just thinking about harrowing Thanksgivings past sends a chill down my spine, and I wonder how different they might have been with a little help. Now, on the drive over, you can open a chatbot and treat it like a life coach.

Give it the persona of your most relentless relative, say, a Fox News-addicted uncle, and practice your responses to off-the-wall questions. Doing a two-minute dry run gets the awkwardness out of your system before you ring the doorbell. I tested this with Claude, feeding it a list of potential landmines, and got back sharp, diplomatic ways to deflect and make light of the moment.

I won’t share them here, but I encourage you to do your own.

Sources indicate that for instance, what if a real-time brouhaha erupts at the table? Instead of letting two relatives shout until everyone is quietly burping into their napkins, whip out a voice-mode AI assistant to act as a neutral referee and break the logjam.

If you are hosting, the stress starts even earlier. Seating arrangements require more diplomacy than a UN General Assembly, and pairing the wrong two cousins guarantees a tug-of-war over the mashed potatoes. Feed your guest list and everyone's friction points into an AI tool, and ask it to build a seating chart that separates natural adversaries with at least two buffers, a centerpiece, or a spot at the kids’ table. (I was single for many years, so that’s where I always ended up.).

You can even have AI generate a custom trivia game to steer conversations away from danger zones like politics, Donald Trump, whether AI will kill us — don’t ask AI about that — or whether the new John Madden movie on Amazon is actually bad or just quirky.

Finally, tension often starts days earlier in the chaotic family group chat, sparked by passive-aggressive comments about who brings what. Instead of firing back a reply you’ll regret on Thursday, paste the thread into an AI assistant and ask it to translate your annoyance into something warm, firm, and drama-free.

Obviously, AI cannot fix deep family dynamics, and it won't miraculously turn my friend’s Oklahoma relatives into MS Now viewers. Still, I told my friend to load up his chatbot before his flight. Between his Fox News uncle and his judgmental great-aunt, having a calm digital wingman in his pocket might be the closest thing he gets to a Thanksgiving miracle.

This article represents the opinions of its writer.

John Casey is a columnist at Raw Story, the Advocate, Daily Beast, and Outsports. He's also the author of Love: The Heroic Stories of Marriage Equality.

#3032. Forget the iPhone Duo and Z Fold 8 – this foldable has it all

📅 21 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 11m • 📚 Deep Dive (2154 w)

Forget the iPhone Duo and Z Fold 8 – this foldable has it all

📅 21 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 11 min read (2154 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Androidcentral

⏱️ ~11 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • According to recent reports, the Xiaomi 18 Fold delivers the best hardware of any passport-style foldable, pairing a lightweight frame with a class-leading battery and a periscope telephoto that outshoots both Apple and Samsung.
  • Class-leading 6,000 mAh battery with fast 67W charging.
  • Versatile triple-camera system with 200MP main camera and 3.5x optical zoom.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, the Xiaomi 18 Fold delivers the best hardware of any passport-style foldable, pairing a lightweight frame with a class-leading battery and a periscope telephoto that outshoots both Apple and Samsung. While HyperOS 4 is fast, fluid, and boasts standout six-app multitasking, its mainland-China-only ROM breaks everyday Western essentials like Android Auto, eSIMs, Find Hub tracking, and Google 2FA prompts. Until Xiaomi gives it the global ROM it deserves, it remains an enthusiast's dream rather than the foldable that everyone should buy, no questions asked.

Lightweight 219 grams passport design.

Class-leading 6,000 mAh battery with fast 67W charging.

Versatile triple-camera system with 200MP main camera and 3.5x optical zoom.

Bright, vivid 5.38-inch cover and 7.58-inch 120Hz LTPO OLED displays.

China-only release with no global ROM.

No Android Auto, no eSIM support.

Broken Google Find Hub and 2FA notifications.

Cannot set Gemini as the default system assistant.

No desktop mode despite wired USB-C video output.

Tinny, treble-heavy speakers and no stylus support.

Why you can trust Android Central Our expert reviewers spend hours testing and comparing products and services so you can choose the best for you. Find out more about how we test.

Cars. Smart Home. Leica-powered cameras. You may have heard of Xiaomi for many reasons, but unless you’re in China, folding phones probably aren't one of them. Yet the manufacturer has been releasing foldables since 2021, experimenting with both flip and book-style designs as it dialed in on what customers actually wanted.

Like Samsung and the Galaxy Z Fold 8, that search led to the passport-style Xiaomi 18 Fold, which debuted days after Apple revealed its own wide foldable. In true Xiaomi fashion, the result is uniquely Xiaomi in both fantastic and not-so-fantastic ways. It feels immediately familiar given its near symmetry with the iPhone Duo, yet it solves some of my biggest complaints with both Apple and Samsung’s foldables.

According to recent reports, both rivals set a precedent that passport-style foldables require compromises compared to traditional flagships. While Xiaomi had to make choices too, it made them in all the right places: battery and cameras. Instead of a smaller cell, you get a 6,000mAh beast – the largest in this form factor. Instead of a dual-lens setup without a telephoto, you get a flagship Leica triple camera complete with a 200MP main sensor and a 3.5x optical periscope telephoto.

Industry observers note that however, the reverse also holds true. Xiaomi’s hardware-first R&D focus – combined with its lack of a global release – means HyperOS 4 lacks the UX refinement and Western polish other brands prioritize. To its credit, Xiaomi made it easy to install Google services and the Play Store, and its take on multitasking is genuinely unique. Still, a couple of daily essentials don't work as intended, and power-user staples like a desktop mode are missing despite support for wired display out.

In a nutshell, the Xiaomi 18 Fold pairs the best hardware in a passport-style foldable with software that falls short in familiar areas.

Call it Xiaomi’s Choice: do you want the absolute best hardware, or slightly lesser hardware with a much more refined software experience? Hardware nerd that I am, its appeal is obvious – though the iPhone Duo being as good as it is makes this a much closer fight than I anticipated.

In mainland China, the Xiaomi 18 Fold starts at 10,999 yuan (roughly $1,640) – undercutting both the $1,899 Galaxy Z Fold 8 and the $1,999 iPhone Duo on paper before grey-market import markups eat into the savings.

Get the latest news from Android Central, your trusted companion in the world of Android.

More frustrating, Xiaomi hosted its global launch event for the Xiaomi 18 Pro and 18 Pro Max earlier this week, conspicuously leaving the 18 Fold behind as a China-only release. This may change in future launches, but sadly, the Xiaomi 18 Fold looks set to remain China-exclusive.

Industry observers note that pick up the Xiaomi 18 Fold, then the iPhone Duo, and the weight difference jumps out immediately. At 219g, Xiaomi's foldable is a full 35g lighter than Apple's first foldable – and only 18g heavier than the Galaxy Z Fold 8, despite cramming in a massive battery and periscope optics. Finished in a stunning matte Nishino Red glass against a dark metal frame, it looks and feels every bit like a premium flagship smartphone.

Industry observers note that looking at raw thickness alone actually sells Xiaomi's engineering short. When you calculate total folded volume, the Xiaomi 18 Fold (105.37 cm³) takes up roughly 6 percent less physical space than the iPhone Duo (111.95 cm³) and even edges out the razor-thin, tall-bodied Oppo Find N6 (105.82 cm³). Only the Galaxy Z Fold 8 (98.43 cm³) and Honor Magic V6 (102.15 cm³) feature smaller overall footprints – and neither offers the combination of a 6,000mAh battery and a periscope telephoto inside a pocket-friendly passport-style chassis.

Even the wide horizontal camera bar works in its favor. Rather than getting in the way, as some have complained, that housing doubles as a natural finger rest and grip mount, giving your index finger a solid ledge to anchor against when using the phone unfolded in portrait mode.

The keel hinge feels sturdy and reassuring, even if it lacks the iPhone Duo's crisp magnetic snap and holds fewer intermediate flex angles. Unlocking is fast and reliable via the side-mounted fingerprint reader, or 2D face unlock – a welcome convenience Apple skipped on the Duo.

Sources indicate that there are inevitably trade-offs in a body that’s just 5.02mm thin when unfolded. The stereo speakers get plenty loud, but they lack low-end warmth and sound noticeably tinny and treble-heavy compared to Samsung and Apple. Unlike the iPhone Duo, it lacks stylus support, and its IP58 rating means it handles water submersion well but lacks the full dust protection of the iPhone Duo.

In a recent development, like the Galaxy Z Fold 8 and iPhone Duo, the wider passport aspect ratio transforms how usable the 18 Fold feels closed. The 5.38-inch cover screen is wide enough for comfortable two-thumb typing without feeling cramped, though it is a touch wide (but manageable) for single-handed use and the heavily rounded outer corners cut slightly more into usable corner real estate than the iPhone Duo's squared-off edges.

Unfold it, and the 7.58-inch inner OLED is a stunner. With HDR brightness pushing well past 3,700 nits, I’ve had no challenges with outdoor visibility in harsh lighting.

According to recent reports, then there’s the crease. There’s no optical illusion here, as Apple has deployed. Instead, the crease virtually disappears straight-on, but is noticeable at sharper viewing angles – and sensitive eyes may notice low-brightness PWM flicker late at night.

The Xiaomi 18 Fold is more than just Xiaomi’s first passport-style foldable; it is also the first phone powered by Xiaomi’s new in-house flagship 3nm XRing O3 chip, paired with 16GB of LPDDR6 RAM.

Sources indicate that in everyday use, it is blisteringly fast, flying through camera processing and split-screen multitasking without a stutter. Push it hard with sustained 3D gaming or prolonged camera sessions, though, and the thin chassis warms up noticeably along the upper half.

Whatever thermal efficiency trade-offs the XRing O3 makes, the 6,000mAh silicon-carbon battery renders them irrelevant. Endurance is class-leading, easily clearing a day of heavy testing. The smaller display sizes – especially the front display – mean lower power draw, with a key net result: the Xiaomi 18 Fold offers the best battery life of any foldable that I’ve tested so far.

When you finally need a top-up, 67W wired charging gets you to 50 percent in 19 minutes and a full charge in 50 minutes (with the brick included in the box). A charge rate of 120 mAh/min means you won’t be left short, and 50W wireless charging also lets you charge fairly quickly without wires.

Recent findings suggest that xiaomi’s hardware-first R&D pays off most on the back. While Apple and Samsung both skipped an optical telephoto lens on their passport foldables, Xiaomi squeezed a 200MP main sensor, a 50MP ultrawide, and a dedicated 50MP 3.5x optical periscope telephoto into the 18 Fold.

As I saw during my head-to-head Dubai Marina camera shootout against the iPhone Duo and Galaxy Z Fold 8, that periscope lens isn't a minor spec-sheet win – it is a blowout. From 3x all the way past 30x, the 18 Fold resolves real optical detail where Apple and Samsung smear into digital mush, while Leica Vibrant color tuning and disciplined low-light metering make it the most consistent shooter of the three passport-style foldables.

The only real camera compromises are a narrower 17mm ultrawide that crops tighter than its rivals and a cover selfie lens that flares in harsh backlighting. Otherwise, this is the closest a squat foldable has come to a true flagship camera system. To dive deeper into the camera, head over to our passport-style foldable camera shootout – you can see some of the zoom examples from that comparison above!

Living with HyperOS 4 (based on Android 17) is a study in contradictions. Strip away the import context, and the software is genuinely lovely to use day to day; animations are fluid, and the UI feels snappy.

Industry observers note that xiaomi's six-app horizontal multitasking strip lets you line up three full-height panes at once while swiping across half a dozen open apps. It’s impressive, and on par with the Oppo Find N6 for the best multitasking on a foldable.

Sources indicate that hyperOS 4 makes it effortless to install Google services, with all the underlying frameworks included out of the box: I have been running the Play Store and the Gemini app on here without a hitch. However, because this device is built strictly for mainland China, several deeply integrated Android features break down in day-to-day usage. It won’t let you swap the default system assistant to launch Gemini, nor change the default browser across the system to Chrome.

Recent findings suggest that then there are Google services. Find Hub demonstrates the device, but can never find its location, even after enabling every background permission. The same applies to Google’s 2FA – when you sign into your Android phone on an existing device, it’ll often prompt you to verify with your existing device. On the Xiaomi 18 Fold, these alerts never appear, even after opening any of Google’s apps.

Then there are two problems common to China-only devices for years. Android Auto simply does not work, and like many China-specific phones, there’s no support for eSIM. This isn’t strictly Xiaomi’s fault, as China only approved eSIMs after Apple forced the issue last year with the eSIM-only iPhone Air launch.

Despite supporting wired video out over USB-C, Xiaomi still omits a desktop mode, third-party app scaling occasionally leaves awkward borders on the 4.24:3 screen, and it doesn't support 6 GHz Wi-Fi.

It has been revealed that the frustrating part is how easy the fix would be. Xiaomi just needs to follow Oppo's playbook and pair the 18 Fold with the Western HyperOS ROM it already shipped globally on the Xiaomi 18 Pro and 18 Pro Max: doing so would wipe out nearly every one of these headaches overnight.

Recent findings suggest that if you want the best hardware in a foldable this size and you can live with the software compromises and compatibility challenges, look no further than the Xiaomi 18 Fold. By pairing a pocketable 219g passport body with a 6,000mAh battery and a Leica periscope camera, Xiaomi proved you don't have to sacrifice flagship hardware for a wide foldable.

According to recent reports, that brings us right back to Xiaomi's Choice. If you live in China – or you are an enthusiast willing to import a phone and live without Android Auto, eSIMs, and Find Hub tracking – this is the finest piece of foldable hardware you can buy.

For everyone else, the iPhone Duo and Galaxy Z Fold 8 remain the safer, far better-integrated daily drivers – even though the hardware is considerably less impressive – at least until Xiaomi finally gives its best foldable the global ROM it deserves.

Personally, the smaller size, excellent battery life, and that telephoto lens mean the Xiaomi 18 Fold will definitely be in my arsenal during trade demonstrates and other work events, even if I keep using the iPhone Duo as my daily passport-style foldable.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Macy's Thanksgiving Day Parade will not be happening on Thanksgiving.
  • According to recent reports, the annual event, which is celebrating its 100th anniversary this year, has been rescheduled for Saturday, Nov.
  • Industry observers note that according to the Weather Channel, Fresh York City is bracing for a nor'easter on Thanksgiving Day.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Macy's Thanksgiving Day Parade will not be happening on Thanksgiving. Yes, you read that correctly.

According to recent reports, the annual event, which is celebrating its 100th anniversary this year, has been rescheduled for Saturday, Nov. 28, due to severe weather.

Industry observers note that according to the Weather Channel, Fresh York City is bracing for a nor'easter on Thanksgiving Day. Before the Macy's Thanksgiving Day Parade was officially rescheduled, officials discussed how the parade could continue. After a 1997 incident where a balloon in the parade crashed into a lamppost and critically injured a bystander, New York City rules state that the parade balloons cannot fly in weather with "sustained winds of 23 mph or gusts of 34 mph.".

The parade has never been postponed before. It has been canceled only three times before, from 1942 to 1944, due to World War II. Balloons in the parade were last grounded 55 years ago, in 1971, due to severe rain and winds.

The annual tradition is televised nationwide on NBC and its affiliates every Thanksgiving.

"The safety of our participants and spectators is our top priority, and after close consultation with our City and agency partners, we have made the decision to move this year’s celebration," Macy’s said in a statement on Wednesday. “Thank you to the thousands of volunteers, performers and partners who create the magic millions enjoy each year. We look forward to celebrating together on Saturday.".

It has been revealed that the Macy's Thanksgiving Parade is now scheduled for 8:30 a.m. ET on Saturday.

The internet, of course, had to react to the unprecedented news.

  • Android Auto has to scale to a lot of different display shapes and sizes, and its functionality varies depending on what you’re using as the platform adapts to what your display can handle.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Google has rolled out a upcoming patch for Android Auto that improves support for wider display formats, but there’s a good chance you won’t be able to see it.

Android Auto has to scale to a lot of different display shapes and sizes, and its functionality varies depending on what you’re using as the platform adapts to what your display can handle. This can sometimes mean you are locked out of a specific feature or need to access it another way. A couple of infamous examples of this include the “Report” option in Google Maps being hidden on smaller displays, as well as the weather card only being on larger, taller displays.

That stated, Google is now making an effort to improve how apps on Android Auto adapters to wider formats.

In a recent development, in the latest app update (v18.2), Android Auto is tweaking apps to switch from a top-bar layout to a sidebar for navigation. So, in Spotify, this means the “Home,” “Recents,” “Browse,” and “Library” shortcuts move to a sidebar rather than being up top.

It’s a good use of space, as it allows more content to be visible on wide but short displays. Android Authority spotted the change across Spotify, YouTube Music, and Phone, implying this is probably a platform-level change rather than being tied to individual app updates.

It’s a great change, but one you might not be able to see.

According to recent reports, as mentioned, Android Auto adjusts to take advantage of whatever display space it has available, and that often includes putting Google Maps off to the side of other apps. While you can easily set Maps to take up the full display, other apps are less likely to be able to do that, with Maps semi-permanently off to the opposite side. In a car with a wide display we tested for this new format, Maps prevented any other apps from going wide enough to show the new layout, so your results may vary. In many cases, this new layout may simply not be visible. In a way, though, that’s a good thing – it reveals that Google is addressing even the most niche aspects of Android Auto, and that’s a win for everyone.

Industry observers note that it’s about time. WhatsApp unveiled today that it is finally adding support for scheduled messages in its app.

In a recent development, A staple of many other messaging apps, WhatsApp is adding scheduled messages to its app. This gives people the ability to write a message but schedule sending it to another user or group chat at a later time.

Scheduled messages on WhatsApp can be sent up to 14 days after you draft them in both 1:1 chats and group chats. You can schedule through a long-press on the send button, with a menu popping up to let you pick the future time when the message will be sent. You can also see scheduled messages before they’re sent to cancel sending or edit the message.

Industry observers note that whatsApp notes that these messages are sent even if your phone’s battery is dead or if the device is off, and everything is still end-to-end encrypted. It works with text, photos, and videos, but apparently not with voice notes.

According to recent reports, that said, the rollout is also scheduled out. WhatsApp claims the feature will start showing up for people “over the coming weeks” globally, so you might be waiting a bit longer for this long overdue release.

Technology stocks fell on Wednesday as excitement over Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang's return faded and failed to calm concerns over the sustainability of the artificial intelligence trade.

Sources indicate that the tech-heavy Nasdaq Composite declined 0.6% and traded off its lows, recovering from steeper losses earlier in the session. Semiconductor stocks dragged on the index, and the VanEck Semiconductor ETF that tracks the sector edged down 1%.

"We just feel that this is panic right now," Venu Krishna, head of U.S. equity strategy at Barclays, told CNBC's "Squawk on the Street" on Wednesday.

"What the market is telling you is that the AI growth narrative has hit a wall and given the centrality of that theme at the economic level, the market is expecting some sort of a macro shock," he added.

After notching one of its best days on record Monday, Nvidia has fallen in the days since and slumped 4% Wednesday. Advanced Micro Devices, Marvell Technology and Intel all edged lower. Micron Technology declined 4%.

Huang's return to Nvidia on Monday briefly revived appetite for tech stocks but didn't fully calm investor concerns over the high costs tied to the AI build-out and worries of a potential slowdown.

Other stocks tied to the AI trade also plummeted. Oracle fell more than 5%. CoreWeave and Nebius moved lower.

AI lab Anthropic bucked the sell-off, however, and climbed more than 4% after shares dropped below last week's blockbuster IPO price.

Wednesday's declines also came as Wall Street digested a hot inflation reading that fueled concerns that higher interest rates could dent demand for growth stocks, including tech.

Amazon and Alphabet each declined about 2%. Microsoft and Tesla lost more than 1% and Meta traded 3% higher.

📅 25 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 5m • 📚 Deep Dive (1004 w)
📖 Baca
Business & Policy ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Ars Technica ↗ Open Full Page

Guilty: Huawei faces steep penalties for stealing T-Mobile, Cisco trade secrets

📅 25 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1004 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Ars Technica

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • On Tuesday, a US jury convicted one of China’s key telecommunications and AI giants, Huawei Technologies, of stealing trade secrets from US tech firms and evading sanctions against Iran.
  • Although the longrunning charges stem back to 2018, the verdict coming now threatens to inflame US-China tensions at a sensitive time, just as Donald Trump prepares to increase tariffs on China.
  • The jury convicted Huawei of charges including bank fraud, conspiracy to defraud the US, money laundering conspiracy, and “substantive” violations of the International Emergency Economic Powers Act.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

On Tuesday, a US jury convicted one of China’s key telecommunications and AI giants, Huawei Technologies, of stealing trade secrets from US tech firms and evading sanctions against Iran.

Although the longrunning charges stem back to 2018, the verdict coming now threatens to inflame US-China tensions at a sensitive time, just as Donald Trump prepares to increase tariffs on China. In a press release, however, the US Department of Justice celebrated the outcome as critical to protecting the US financial system, the global telecommunications industry, and US national security.

The jury convicted Huawei of charges including bank fraud, conspiracy to defraud the US, money laundering conspiracy, and “substantive” violations of the International Emergency Economic Powers Act.

Among crimes, Huawei was found guilty of “repeatedly” lying to banks about its business in Iran. Huawei also frequently lied to the US government that “it did not assist Iran’s government, military, or intelligence community,” the DOJ said. In reality, the DOJ proved at trial that Huawei was conducting business in Iran under the name “Skycom” to evade sanctions, while providing Iran with “turnkey services with respect to an Internet backbone and broader accessibility for mobile networks.” Further, Huawei helped the Iranian regime “monitor and censor its consumers’ access to the Internet” and provided surveillance cameras to monitor protests, the DOJ said. In a statement, the acting principal deputy assistant attorney general for national security, M. Scott Proctor, said Huawei “empowered our enemies” and “harmed our national security.”.

As the DOJ successfully argued, Huawei lied about its Iranian business specifically so that it could continue obtaining billions in US dollars by participating in a global marketplace that gave it necessary access to steal US tech. Among companies targeted, US Attorney for the Eastern District of Upcoming York Joseph Nocella Jr. noted that Huawei blatantly stole from T-Mobile and Cisco, as well as a semiconductor storage organization called CNEX and an antenna manufacturer called Quintel.

Industry observers note that one of the stolen ideas was the design of a T-Mobile robot called “Tappy,” which helped the US firm “assess the responsiveness of touch screens by mimicking a human touch,” the DOJ remarked. To copy the design, Huawei signed a non-disclosure agreement, then sent photos and technical details back to China. Even bolder, when that intel was deemed insufficient, “a Huawei employee stole a part of the robot in his backpack and carried it out of T-Mobile’s controlled laboratory,” the DOJ said.

Huawei’s tactics weren’t always sophisticated, but they were effective, the DOJ stated, building into “a long-running conspiracy to steal intellectual property of US companies.” At trade reveals and tours of rivals’ facilities, Huawei employees would pretend to “get lost,” the DOJ said, so they could wander into restricted areas and take photos of hardware, The Latest York Times reported.

Huawei engineers would also sometimes hide their activity by spelling words backwards. For example, Huawei was able to copy the source code used on Cisco routers—which the DOJ noted was “identified as the ‘crown jewel’ of Cisco technology”—by taking notes in which they spelled Cisco as “ocsic.” Another time, the DOJ noted that a Huawei employee was caught “photographing proprietary Fujitsu equipment” while wearing a badge that falsely identified him as an employee of “Weihua.”.

During the trial, Meredith Arfa, a federal prosecutor, noted that Huawei employees were sometimes paid bonuses for their crimes, since the theft was so integral to Huawei’s business model, NYT reported.

Roman Rozhavsky, the assistant director of the FBI’s Counterintelligence and Espionage Division, stated that Huawei spent years expanding its international enterprise “through theft of trade secrets, fraud, and other criminal conduct at the expense of US companies and the rule of law.”.

It has been revealed that huawei has been banned from selling its tech in the US since 2019, so NYT noted that the guilty verdict is unlikely to rattle the organization’s finances much. However, the financial penalties stemming from the verdict could be steep, as the DOJ explained that they include “criminal fines, forfeiture, and restitution.”.

Sentencing is scheduled for September 14.

Huawei continues to deny any wrongdoing and rejects US claims that the Chinese Communist Party directed the thefts. NYT noted that Huawei’s investors have argued that the US fight is politically motivated and seeks to hobble “a Chinese initiative to build 5G networks around the world.”.

Outside the courthouse following the verdict, Brian Heberlig, a lawyer for Huawei, told reporters that it’s significant that the jury did not convict Huawei of racketeering charges or conspiracy to obstruct justice. According to Heberlig, the examples of US technology theft merely represented “isolated misconduct by firm employees,” which inevitably happens in a company so large, with “hundreds of thousands of people.”.

Heberlig confirmed that Huawei planned to appeal and considered the jury’s opposition to racketeering charges to be a “profound rejection of the United States’ narratives about what Huawei is.”.

“The allegations that the government made in this case overreached and simply weren’t consistent with the successful, innovative and hard-working company that we came to know and deeply respect in this trial,” Heberlig mentioned.

In a recent development, after the verdict, China “lashed out” at the US, AFP reported. According to Chinese foreign ministry spokesperson Guo Jiakun, the US is trying to use the ruling to “suppress” Huawei.

China “firmly opposes the US suppressing and containing Chinese enterprises and firmly supports Chinese enterprises in safeguarding their legitimate rights and interests,” Guo said.

However, the FBI’s Rozhavsky suggested that even China, which frequently negotiates with Trump as the trade rivals continually clash, can’t spare Huawei from substantial penalties.

“This case serves as a stark reminder that the Chinese government continues to pose a serious threat to our economic and national security, but today’s guilty verdict proves the FBI and our partners will aggressively investigate, expose, and hold accountable those who target our nation,” Rozhavsky said. “No firm is too substantial, too powerful, or too well connected to exploit the US and its citizens and expect to escape American justice.”.

Latest Update: Study: Meta settlement needs YouTube, TikTok to succeed

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • When Meta settled a massive social media addiction lawsuit brought by multiple state attorneys general in August, it invited YouTube and TikTok to join the terms.
  • Meta, which agreed to implement latest restrictions on teen use, argued that the safeguards amounted to a new industry standard.
  • Recent findings suggest that "These protections will only be truly effective if we work with our peers — TikTok and YouTube — to put the same measures in place," Meta remarked in a statement at the time.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

When Meta settled a massive social media addiction lawsuit brought by multiple state attorneys general in August, it invited YouTube and TikTok to join the terms.

Meta, which agreed to implement latest restrictions on teen use, argued that the safeguards amounted to a new industry standard. They included a two-hour daily time limit, removing nighttime access to Meta apps by default, and no notifications during school hours.

Recent findings suggest that "These protections will only be truly effective if we work with our peers — TikTok and YouTube — to put the same measures in place," Meta remarked in a statement at the time. Neither social media platform has joined the settlement since.

Now, a new study published in JAMA suggests Meta was right about the potential effect of YouTube and TikTok agreeing to the restrictions.

Industry observers note that the authors analyzed existing data from ongoing research known as the Adolescent Brain Cognitive Development (ABCD) Study, which tracks teen screen time and social media habits. They looked at data from 1,803 participants over a five-year period between Nov. 2020 and Aug. 2025.

Industry observers note that they found the Meta apps Instagram and Facebook accounted for only 20 percent of total daily social media use amongst those participants. Snapchat, TikTok, and YouTube comprised the remaining apps named in the litigation.

Additionally, the authors found that significantly more teens would benefit from the time limit, nighttime access, and notification restrictions if the other companies implemented them.

It has been revealed that "I think many people hailed that settlement with a huge sigh of relief, but unless the other companies join suit, these data suggest it's not going to make a huge difference," Dr. Dimitri Christakis, principal investigator at the Center for Child Health, Behavior and Development at Seattle Children's, said in a statement. (Christakis has served as an expert witness in social media litigation and has received consulting fees from the attorneys general of California, Newly introduced Mexico, Virginia, and Washington.) If you buy something through links on our site, Mashable may earn an affiliate commission.

The Apple iPhone 18 Pro is free right now with T-Mobile.

Industry observers note that dr. Jason Nagata, an associate professor of pediatrics at the University of California, San Francisco who was not involved in the study, said the real-world phone-use data allowed the authors to examine how the settlement's proposed protections might come into play.

Sources indicate that the daily time limit, for example, would affect just 7.7 percent of teens in the ABCD study. If implemented by TikTok, YouTube, and Snapchat, that would rise to 63 percent.

Blocking Meta access from midnight to 6 a.m. would affect more than three-quarters of Meta owners. By contrast, the same rule applied to TikTok, YouTube, and Snapchat would cover nearly 90 percent of users in the ABCD study.

Recent findings suggest that there's a similar disparity for overnight notifications. Shutting them off between 10 p.m. and 7 a.m. would affect almost two-thirds of Meta owners, but 86 percent across TikTok, YouTube, Snapchat, Facebook, and Instagram.

"The study shows how difficult it can be to address social media use one manufacturer at a time when teens regularly move across many different platforms," noted Nagata, who previously used ABCD data to study smartphone use at night and during school.

Recent findings suggest that nagata noted that the JAMA study doesn't indicate how well the proposed restrictions will work in the real world. Teens might change their behavior, shift to other platforms, or develop workarounds. Nagata believes future research must evaluate which restrictions reduce problematic use and improve teen health and well-being.

The authors acknowledged other key limitations in their research. The ABCD study sample included only Android users, not iPhone users, so it may not reflect the experiences of all U.S. teens. The passive phone tracking may miss use on other devices like tablets or laptops. The study didn't capture the content viewed by users, which may affect teens differently. The estimated reach of the restrictions is also hypothetical.

Still, the researchers argue their estimates provide a baseline for understanding the restrictions' potential impact.

"The settlement will affect some teenagers but not enough,” Christakis mentioned.

Google has already taken its first steps toward putting compute into space, with the launch of a “Project Suncatcher” AI server satellite last month. Jeff Bezos’ Blue Origin will carry out the first dedicated heavy-lift launch for Project Suncatcher in 2029.

💡 Key Takeaways

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Nvidia chip sellers are seeking latest buyers for the semiconductor giant's hardware, three people told CNBC, after the Trump administration tightened rules to curb Chinese companies' remote access to the most advanced artificial-intelligence systems.

According to recent reports, companies have put an unusually high volume of Nvidia graphics processing units, or GPUs, on the market since new measures restricting Chinese companies renting access to advanced Nvidia chips were declared on Nov. 16, the people stated.

Jack Duhamel, president of AI infrastructure marketplace GPU Mart, and two people familiar with the matter told CNBC the surge in GPUs for sale was directly attributable to the newly introduced rule. Duhamel added that one company looking to sell Nvidia chips told GPU Mart the sale was related to the new rule.

The two people stated it appeared chip sellers were seeking to offload them because they were originally for use in data centers in which Chinese companies would rent access. They asked not to be named because they were discussing private information.

The Department of Commerce's Bureau of Industry and Security, or BIS, confirmed an interim final rule as part of a clampdown on Chinese companies bypassing export controls, which effectively ban the sale of the most advanced Nvidia chips to China, by accessing them remotely in overseas data centers. The rule came into effect on Nov. 19.

Deals to find buyers for thousands of B300 GPUs, one of Nvidia's most advanced offerings, have been floated since the rule was unveiled, noted Duhamel and one of the people.

Nvidia declined to comment. BIS did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

Nvidia has been facing increasing scrutiny from U.S. lawmakers over Chinese companies' access to its advanced chips.

Recent findings suggest that the chip giant warned its customers that the proposed Remote Access Security Act — which has passed the House of Representatives but is yet to pass the Senate — would give the U.S. government broader authority to control access to cloud services, potentially exposing both parties to "legal action," sources previously told CNBC.

It has been revealed that in July, the U.S. accused a Chinese AI lab, Moonshot AI, of accessing Nvidia chips via a facility in Thailand. CNBC reported on Nov. 5 that the tech giant had sought access to the chips via data centers in Europe.

U.S. Trade Representative Jamieson Greer told CNBC's "Squawk Box" on Wednesday that the fresh rule confirmed last week was intended to close "loopholes.".

"For a long time, we have not allowed the sale of Blackwell chips, which are the highest AI chips or similar chips to China directly," he remarked.

"Some rules were issued by the Commerce Department last week to close off indirect access, either smuggling through places like Southeast Asia or remote access from data centers in third countries.".

During Nvidia's third-quarter earnings call on Nov. 17, then-interim CEO Colette Kress said the tech giant was still studying the controls, but expected performance to remain strong because demand for chips far exceeded supply.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

WhatsApp on Wednesday started rolling out a much-sought-after feature: the ability to schedule messages in both individual and group chats.

The feature is rolling out globally to all consumers across iOS and Android. Once it becomes available, you can type a message and long-press the send button to schedule it. You can choose to send a message anywhere between 10 minutes and 14 days later.

Recent findings suggest that people will be able to see all their scheduled messages and delete them if needed. It’s not clear if there is a way to edit the schedule of a message.

Recent findings suggest that notably, scheduled messages will be sent even if your phone is off or outside network coverage. You can schedule messages containing text, photos, and videos.

It has been revealed that the feature could prove useful for wishing someone a happy birthday on time or chatting with people across time zones. Businesses may also find it easier to schedule texts and updates to their customers, and people who use the app to coordinate work will likely find themselves using scheduled texts to update their teams.

WhatsApp rivals like Telegram and Signal have had the ability to schedule messages for a while now, so the Meta-owned chat app is late in rolling it out.

📅 25 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 3m • 📚 Deep Dive (687 w)

General ⚠️ Warning 🌐 Ars Technica ↗ Open Full Page

Latest Update: Ars Live recap: Don’t expect military attacks on data centers to stop

📅 25 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (687 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Ars Technica

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • In a recent development, amazon data centers came under military attack for the first time ever in the Middle East this year, and Russia and Ukraine exchanged an unprecedented flurry of drone strikes on each other’s data centers.
  • In a conversation with Ars Technica Tech Reporter Jeremy Hsu, Joseph Jarnecki at the Royal United Services Institute first talked about why public cloud data centers have increasingly become military targets during the 2026 Iran war and the ongoing full-scale Russian invasion of Ukraine:.
  • We see an increasing acknowledgement and fact of dual use in particularly the public cloud, but also just across the board in private cloud data centers as well.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, amazon data centers came under military attack for the first time ever in the Middle East this year, and Russia and Ukraine exchanged an unprecedented flurry of drone strikes on each other’s data centers. To examine what such attacks on data centers mean for the future of cloud services that all modern societies depend upon, Ars hosted a live discussion.

In a conversation with Ars Technica Tech Reporter Jeremy Hsu, Joseph Jarnecki at the Royal United Services Institute first talked about why public cloud data centers have increasingly become military targets during the 2026 Iran war and the ongoing full-scale Russian invasion of Ukraine:.

We see an increasing acknowledgement and fact of dual use in particularly the public cloud, but also just across the board in private cloud data centers as well. The dual use that I refer to is the utilization of compute functions within these data centers—within cloud services—by militaries, for example, to run battlefield management systems, to do their HR, to do their resource management. Once a military uses a piece of civilian infrastructure, at least under international law or in terms of the principles of targeting that are taken forward by militaries, it can sometimes become a military object and is therefore of interest to an adversary, and there’s an incentive to target it.

Jarnecki also highlighted the fact that relatively cheap kamikaze drones can inflict disproportionate economic costs and create widespread cloud disruptions when striking data centers:.

The second reason that we’ve seen targeting particularly in Russia’s largest data centers or some of Russia’s largest public cloud data centers like Yandex, as well as American hyperscalers that are based in the Gulf, is to impose economic cost in a way that would be disadvantageous for an adversary and would otherwise be quite difficult to impose in other ways. So it’s relatively low cost of munition to high cost of disruption. If you think about the amount of investment that’s been put forward by AWS and other companies in the Gulf to build out these data center installations relative to the cost of the amount of Shahed drones that are manufactured, produced, and utilized by Iran to target these data centers, I would put it very, very conservatively at 100X or even more. The cost ratio is really very lucrative for the adversary, and it provides the opportunity to really degrade the economic outcomes of who you are targeting.

Much of the discussion also focused on cloud resilience lessons for both governments and hyperscalers, with the latter including large cloud and data center operators such as Amazon, Google, Microsoft, and Meta. Jarnecki highlighted the example of how Ukraine took steps to safeguard its cloud infrastructure when Russian President Vladimir Putin ordered Russian military forces to launch the full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022:.

I think that Ukraine anticipated this problem set very effectively. They anticipated and understood that Russia would not be discriminating necessarily in its targeting of civilian digital infrastructure particularly, and therefore conducted a large-scale cloud migration at the onset of the full-scale war in part in reaction to the anticipated targeting but then also actual targeting that took place through kinetic means.

Such lessons are vital because 2026 is unlikely to be the last year in which data centers come under substantial military attack, Jarnecki stated:.

It has been revealed that unfortunately, I think that this really does indicate a continuation of this kind of targeting, not just because data centers are, despite efforts to harden some of them, relatively squishy, relatively easy to find, and have the potential, because of their complexity, to induce cascading risks within the facility or more widely if they are hit particularly by kinetic munitions. So at present, I would say it’s a dangerous trend that is likely to crop up again.

Throughout the event, Jarnecki also addressed viewer questions about whether data centers can realistically be hardened or built underground to withstand physical attacks, and even how orbital data centers or low-Earth orbit satellite constellations such as Starlink could provide backup options from space.

The loneliest peptide party in New York

📅 25 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 10 min read (1971 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: The Verge

⏱️ ~10 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • The peptide curious are looking for answers, and finding dubious products instead.﻿.
  • In a recent development, this is Optimizer, a weekly newsletter sent from Verge senior reviewer Victoria Song that dissects and discusses the latest gizmos and potions that swear they’re going to change your life.
  • Recent findings suggest that on a rainy fall evening, an experimental art venue in Chelsea Market had a small line out the door.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The peptide curious are looking for answers, and finding dubious products instead.﻿.

Photography by Jack Califano / The Verge.

In a recent development, this is Optimizer, a weekly newsletter sent from Verge senior reviewer Victoria Song that dissects and discusses the latest gizmos and potions that swear they’re going to change your life. Opt in for Optimizer here.

Recent findings suggest that on a rainy fall evening, an experimental art venue in Chelsea Market had a small line out the door. There are always lines in Newly introduced York City. Viral food trends, gallery exhibitions, pop-ups, and parties. The folks in line looked like your average joe, ready for a Friday night on the town. You wouldn’t look twice — except, perhaps, for a man with a wizard beard and a laser sword strapped to his back.

Inside, the man with a laser sword stood in the middle of the cavernous bottom floor of a two-story warehouse strewn with large bean bags. On the wall were psychedelic projections of jellyfish, shrimp, and other sea creatures. A bizarre choice, considering peptides won’t induce any trippy vision quests, and not a single person was getting groovy. The industrial beams had posters with QR codes that you could scan to get samples of Afterglow, a new type of peptide product. According to seemingly discarded pamphlets around the venue, Afterglow isn’t a standard injectable or oral peptide. The firm makes strips that dissolve under the tongue. The “Afterglow Peptide Field Guide” also described what each sample does, dosing recommendations, and potential side effects. At the upstairs bar, bartenders mixed custom cocktails called Afterburn — complete with bioluminescent veggie nectar — and Margatrutide. (For the record, a bioluminescent veggie nectar cocktail tastes as awful as you think.).

Welcome to a peptide launch party.

Sources indicate that peptide parties are old news in San Francisco, but they’re somewhat more novel in Upcoming York City. Milling around the edges of the venue were various reporters and photographers. We were all trying to get a sense of why anyone had bothered to come out. Not that many did. Despite the venue’s size, the main floor had plenty of empty space.

One person I spoke to was a fencer with sore joints. They’d heard that one of the peptides might help with recovery. Another had a father in the wellness industry and had heard vague things about how effective peptides could be. One woman, staring at a projected jellyfish, merely shrugged. Her friend was more into “wellness stuff” and she had no intends, so, why not check out a party? A man, staring into his bag of Afterglow samples, was mostly interested in weight loss but scared about the safety of gray market products. A few feet away, another man was furiously reading the Afterglow pamphlet. “I like to know what I put in my body,” he stated.

The only problem was he didn’t remember which sample he had tried.

A common refrain: Well, this beats doing research online. This, at least, was a social event where you could theoretically connect with other people. And there were clusters of strangers speaking to each other. Mostly, near the bar. Everywhere else, people stared awkwardly on their phones, their eyes occasionally roaming the room without meeting anyone else’s gaze for more than a second or two. After a while, they’d disappear into the back room and reappear with a goody bag full of peptide samples.

After 90 minutes, I decided to leave. For the umpteenth time that evening, I’d walked up to someone, asked about peptides, and got a noncommittal “I really don’t know anything — I just came to learn more.” (When asked if they had, they invariably shrugged and pointed to the goody bag.) It was clear that the only peptide evangelists here were likely associated with the launch. The whole thing, to me, seemed as if someone had tried to draw a cool party from memory. The last thing I saw was a person draped in a ghost sheet sitting alone in the corner.

Sources indicate that as it turned out, the man with the laser sword was a performance artist who’d been invited to attend. Out of journalistic integrity, I asked if he had ever tried peptides. He told me he was more interested in the unifying energy of the universe. When I got up to leave, he waved and mentioned, “Giggles.”.

If I were peptide curious, the Afterglow launch party was a pretty awful way to learn anything about these substances. To be fair, Afterglow’s Partiful invitation mostly described this event as “an environment great for aura farming” and the “hard launch of [its] first of many experiments in culture.” Nevertheless, as part of the press, I did walk away with a smattering of Afterglow’s products. In total, I got packets of what Afterglow calls Charge (NAD+), Rejuvenate (glutathione), Wolverine Blend (BPC-157 / TB-500), Strength Blend (CJC-1295 / Ipamorelin), Glow Blend (GHK-Cu / BPC-157 / TB-500), Connect (PT-141), GLP-2 (tirzepatide), and GLP-3 (retatrutide). Or at least that’s what the packaging states. There’s no way to truly verify gray market peptides for safety or efficacy because they’re unregulated products.

Industry observers note that first of all, last I checked, GLP-1 medications do not upgrade like iPhone models. Afterglow’s pamphlet correctly lists that your body has “three hormone switches”: GLP-1, GIP, and glucagon. The accompanying descriptors of what each does are broadly correct, though lacking in nuance. For example, there is a hormone called glucagon-like peptide 2, but it’s not tirzepatide. The “real” GLP-2 is a hormone related to intestinal health. Tirzepatide is still considered a GLP-1 medication that’s a dual agonist because it works on two hormones (GLP-1 and GIP.) The GLP-2 moniker is a misnomer popularized by ill-informed influencers. The same goes for retatrutide, which, as of this writing, is still an unapproved GLP-1 medication that works on three hormones (GLP-1, GIP, and glucagon) and is therefore a triple agonist. There is no such thing as GLP-3.

For all the samples, there were no instructions regarding dosing on the packaging — just another QR code leading to Afterglow’s product page. Those pages happen to contain instructions for how to use the strips, and the amount of product within the strips. There are disclaimers about how little studied the compounds are, but nothing about interactions, side effects, or what to expect while taking. Just a throwaway line to talk to your doctor.

Sources indicate that all that information, you’d have to find on the pamphlet given at the party. (Ironically, some “vital cautions” on the pamphlet state to avoid taking samples with alcohol, at a party where the booze was flowing.) Provided you didn’t throw it out. One would hope that information is on a box if you were to buy directly from the seller. But for all intents and purposes, what I just described is what a clueless partygoer would have to go on.

If everything in that pamphlet were 100 percent factual, perhaps a conscientious partygoer could feel reassured. On that front, I have bad news. The pamphlet calls PT-141 an “FDA-approved peptide that boosts sexual desire for both men and women.”.

Recent findings suggest that PT-141, also known as bremelanotide or Vyleesi, is FDA approved. But only for premenopausal women suffering from hypoactive sexual desire disorder. It is not approved for post-menopausal women, men, or for general sexual performance enhancement.

Another concern: How does one evaluate a sublingual peptide strip? Specifically, is this delivery method even scientifically proven effective in humans? Spoiler: It’s not! A collapsible FAQ menu on Afterglow’s site states, “We don’t know yet. Nobody has published how much of most peptides reaches the blood from a strip compared with an injection. We’re funding studies to measure exactly that, and we’ll share what we find.”.

As for why you’d want to even try a sublingual strip? Afterglow’s website suggests it’s more convenient than injections or pills. No refrigeration, no needles, and no need for learning how to reconstitute a drug. Just pop a strip under the tongue and go.

According to recent reports, and good luck trying to find reputable sources of information on your own. Afterglow says it’s funding its own research, but its site has no reviewable documentation just yet. A Google search brings up a questionable AI overview, a handful of links from dubious med spas, a couple of dead links, and one PubMed study in mice. Most of the links also primarily discuss the difference between oral peptides in pill form and injectables — so not terribly relevant here.

Recent findings suggest that I’d consider it fair game if I were confident that anyone at the party I went to did their due diligence. As it stands, I talked with over a dozen people who were mostly there for vibes, booze, and freebies.

In a recent development, not all peptide parties are created equal. Some happen on WWII cargo ships, complete with panel discussions about peptide supply chains. Another “peptide 101” talk I attended in Latest York happened at the back of a bitcoin bar. There, most attendees also knew very little about peptides, but at least they got treated to a PowerPoint presentation about the basics. There was a dubious demonstration of how to inject oneself that would’ve probably made any pharmacist or doctor scream. But at the very least, peptides were defined and attendees could ask questions. (The answers to those questions were on the right track with regard to the dangers of the gray market. They were less reliable about scientific rigor and why “anecdotal evidence” is not the same as clinical evidence of safety.).

But a striking, recurring theme is just how much is unknown. These substances aren’t well-studied in humans, so there’s not much evidence as to long-term benefits or side effects. The peptide curious know shocking little about the substances they’re supposedly interested in. Likewise, it’s incredibly difficult to get reliable, unbiased data on gray market interest or usage, though there have been attempts to quantify this surging demand in recent months. Case in point, telehealth provider Hims & Hers just conducted a consumer survey of roughly 2,000 American adults. Of those surveyed, 68 percent said they had little to no knowledge about peptides. Less than 18 percent were even able to identify that peptides are chains of amino acids. Even so, 40 percent said they were interested or very interested in trying injectable prescription treatments — including peptides — if offered by a telehealth service.

According to recent reports, even so, peptides are everywhere. The word appears in copious ads for skincare creams, weight loss drugs, and supplements. Looksmaxxers, influencers, and celebrities like Gwyneth Paltrow and Joe Rogan talk about them in podcasts, documentaries, and social media as if they’re miracle shortcuts. Hims & Hers has even announced it’s launching a service called Peptide Plus — nevermind that the vast majority of what it’ll offer are not actual peptides.

In this kind of environment, of course more people will become peptide curious. Which makes it even more concerning that the most readily available information sources are not medical or scientific experts well-versed on the topic at hand. There are dubious links online summarized into less-than-critical AI overviews. There are pamphlets handed out at weird parties, where there’s more booze and schmooze than education. Influencers branding themselves as experts as they flash crudely summarized studies in a bar back room. Industry panels that are inaccessible to the average consumer, full of jargon and assumed knowledge of the science at hand.

Recent findings suggest that it’s clear something needs to be done until general knowledge improves. Until then, the parties will continue.

According to recent reports, X announced new creation tools Wednesday, many of them focused on short-form vertical video. The updates are part of the platform’s effort to compete with social networks such as YouTube and Instagram as the format continues to grow in popularity.

Recent findings suggest that the tools are designed to help creators make professional-quality vertical videos, share original content more easily, and earn more. They also give creators more ways to record, edit, and publish content directly on the platform without relying on third-party apps.

Sources indicate that A key addition is an upgraded media editor that lets creators produce polished vertical videos without leaving X. Recording features include the ability to capture video in segments and use green-screen effects, the company said.

The editor also offers a range of postproduction tools. Creators can convert horizontal videos to vertical format, automatically generate captions, trim footage, add text overlays, choose custom thumbnails, and adjust photos before publishing.

Thanks to a recently announced update, customers can now add up to 20 photos and videos to a single post, which audiences can swipe through horizontally. X says the feature is intended for sharing event recaps, behind-the-scenes moments, and product rolls out.

Availability of the new features varies by region, X stated.

In a recent development, earlier this month, the company introduced a clipping feature that lets users take snippets from longer videos, add their own commentary, and post the clips without leaving X. Clips credit and link to the original video, plus the person who creates a clip and the original poster can earn from its views.

According to recent reports, another feature, “React with Video,” launched earlier this year. Similar to TikTok’s “stitch” feature, this lets creators respond to posts with video commentary while displaying the original post in the background.

X has also introduced upcoming earning opportunities and updates to its creator monetization programs in recent months. These include the “Video Kickstart Bonus,” an invitation-only pilot that rewards selected creators for publishing original vertical videos under three minutes long and without watermarks.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • What happens to your private conversations when an AI company goes bankrupt?

  • Industry observers note that the attorneys general involved in the matter have put out individual press releases, claiming that Character.ai’s dataset includes chat histories from more than 21 million U.S.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

What happens to your private conversations when an AI company goes bankrupt? If it’s Character.ai, apparently, the blueprint is to auction them off to the highest bidder.

Now, a coalition of 42 state attorneys general is intervening in Character.ai’s bankruptcy proceedings in an effort to stop the chatbot maker from selling off sensitive user data, which includes the private conversations of millions of users.

Industry observers note that the attorneys general involved in the matter have put out individual press releases, claiming that Character.ai’s dataset includes chat histories from more than 21 million U.S. accounts, more than 2.1 million of which belong to minors. In addition, the sale would involve other personal data, like IP addresses, the statements said.

Only one anonymous bidder for the chat data has been disclosed so far: Smirks and Pangs Acquisition LLC (Smirks), which was set up as a Delaware company on November 13, 2026. The following day, Character.ai picked it as the base bid for the auction, scheduled for December 1, California Attorney General Rob Bonta noted. It is unclear what the buyer’s plans are for the chats.

In addition, some states, including California, Colorado, Fresh York, and Connecticut, have enacted chatbot safety legislation that will go into effect on January 1, 2027, which could trigger further violations if the sale goes through.

“Character.AI promised consumers that their data would not be sold. This kind of behavior is illegal under federal and California law and bankruptcy should not be used to sidestep these consumer protections,” Bonta said in a statement.

Connecticut Attorney General William Tong also criticized Character.ai’s business model.

It has been revealed that “Their chatbots drove vulnerable youth down a rabbit hole of emotionally volatile and sexually inappropriate chats,” Tong said. “Their reckless misconduct and broken business model drove their firm into the ground. Now they want to abuse the bankruptcy process to do exactly what they said they wouldn’t do — auction off those private chat records and personal details to a shady buyer.”.

Tong added: “We objected to the Disney sale, and we’re calling on the bankruptcy court to reject this sale too as yet another guise to eviscerate legal liability and consumer protection.”.

According to recent reports, the opposition to the Disney sale was led by a similar but not identical coalition of state AGs. They fought against a proposed $20 million licensing deal that would give Disney access to Character.ai’s intellectual property, but not to consumers’ chats. The deal has not yet received final court approval. (Disney also agreed to hire most of Character.ai’s remaining staff.).

In a recent development, character.ai suffered after its co-founders, Noam Shazeer and Daniel De Freitas, returned to Google, when the tech giant signed a non-exclusive license to use the AI startup’s tech. The company also faced lawsuits related to child safety — one involved the suicide of a 14-year-old Florida boy whose mother claimed he had become obsessed with a chatbot on the platform.

California AG Bonta is joined in the effort to oppose the sale of Character.ai user data by attorneys general from Alaska, Arkansas, Colorado, Connecticut, the District of Columbia, Delaware, Florida, Georgia, Hawaii, Idaho, Illinois, Indiana, Kansas, Kentucky, Louisiana, Maine, Maryland, Michigan, Minnesota, Mississippi, Missouri, Nevada, Latest Hampshire, New Jersey, New York, North Carolina, North Dakota, Ohio, Oklahoma, Oregon, Pennsylvania, Rhode Island, South Carolina, South Dakota, Tennessee, Utah, Virginia, Vermont, Washington, Wisconsin, and West Virginia.

Industry observers note that according to a new Counterpoint Research report, Apple increased its share of Latin America’s smartphone shipments in Q3 2026, recording the smallest decline among the region’s top five brands. Here are the details.

In a report released this week, Counterpoint Research states the ongoing memory crunch led to a 24% year-over-year drop in smartphone shipments during Q3, “the second-lowest quarter since 2015.”.

Sources indicate that per the report, Samsung maintained its lead with a 35% shipment share, despite a 15% year-over-year decline in total shipments, well ahead of second-place Motorola, which captured 18% of shipments after a 23% drop. Interestingly, Motorola’s share actually increased one percentage point from a year earlier.

Rounding out the top five were Xiaomi, with a 14% share and a whopping 34% decline, Apple, with a 9% share and a 10% decline, and Honor, with an 8% share and a 27% decline.

Despite the decline in overall shipments, Apple’s shipment share increased by 2 percentage points from 7% a year earlier, moving the manufacturer from fifth to fourth place in the region.

Other brands collectively accounted for 16% of shipments, down from 19% a year earlier, with their combined shipments falling 37% year over year.

Here’s Counterpoint on Apple’s performance for Q3 in Latin America:.

Sources indicate that apple was the most resilient, with the smallest decline among the top five brands (shipments down 10% YoY), and rose one position to No. 4 in the region. Apple absorbed the impact of price increases better than its rivals, helped by strong product availability. Apple introduced the iPhone 18 Pro series at the end of the quarter. For the first time, Chile joined Brazil and Mexico in the first launch wave.

Industry observers note that as for regional factors that contributed to the decline, Senior Analyst Benjamin Corona noted that Brazil, Mexico, and Colombia faced additional challenges beyond the global memory shortage, ranging from political uncertainty to inflation and tighter household budgets. Smartphone shipments fell 22%, 26%, and 28% in those countries, respectively.

Looking ahead, Counterpoint says it “expects the decline to ease in Q4 2026 as prices stabilize and seasonal demand returns,” adding that “memory-related price pressure should moderate by Q2 2027, but supply constraints will likely continue through the end of 2027.”.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Abdulrahman Alfozan, the Saudi national accused of bugging an executive conference room at OpenAI's headquarters, has been released from custody, his attorney told CNBC on Wednesday.
  • The confirmation of Alfozan's release came a day after a federal judge in San Francisco noted the defendant would be allowed out of jail on a $1 million bond, despite prosecutors' warnings that he posed a serious flight risk.
  • Alfozan, a former OpenAI engineer, is expected to be fitted with an ankle monitor, his attorney, David Rizk, previously told CNBC.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Abdulrahman Alfozan, the Saudi national accused of bugging an executive conference room at OpenAI's headquarters, has been released from custody, his attorney told CNBC on Wednesday.

The confirmation of Alfozan's release came a day after a federal judge in San Francisco noted the defendant would be allowed out of jail on a $1 million bond, despite prosecutors' warnings that he posed a serious flight risk.

Alfozan, a former OpenAI engineer, is expected to be fitted with an ankle monitor, his attorney, David Rizk, previously told CNBC.

Alfozan was scheduled to be released from detention Wednesday morning at 8 a.m. PT. Shortly before that deadline, U.S. Attorney Craig Missakian of the Northern District of California urged the court to maintain Alfozan's detention pending trial, "given the significant risk that the defendant will flee to Saudi Arabia if he is released from custody.".

In an order posted on the case docket later Wednesday, Judge Vince Chhabria stated the court only learned of the government's last-minute bid to block Alfozan's release after he had already been let out.The government's motion "is therefore denied as moot," Chhabria's order stated. The judge set a hearing for Dec. 3 on the bid to revoke the magistrate judge's order releasing Alfozan.

Pointing to Alfozan's "ample resources, significant family and professional ties to Saudi Arabia, and few remaining ties to the United States," Missakian had argued in a court filing that the release conditions imposed by Magistrate Judge Alex Tse "are insufficient to safeguard the defendant's appearance for future proceedings in this case.".

Alfozan "presents a serious risk of flight that no set of release conditions can reasonably mitigate," Missakian wrote.

According to recent reports, his office sought to pause the magistrate judge's release order until a ruling on a motion to revoke it. The Department of Justice did not immediately respond to CNBC's request for comment on Alfozan's release.

It has been revealed that tse in a court hearing Tuesday ruled in favor of Rizk's motion for his client's release, which noted prosecutors have admitted finding "no fresh evidence to support the theory that Mr. Alfozan was stealing trade secrets, or to support the speculation that he was acting as an unregistered foreign agent for Saudi Arabia.".

It has been revealed that in a text message to CNBC after that hearing, Rizk stated, "We are simply grateful that the Court made the right decision to release Mr. Alfozan and now we look forward to defending the case.".

But Missakian's filing Wednesday morning pushed back, saying "the government's investigation of this seven-week-old case is ongoing.".

Prosecutors have so far found "hundreds of audio files" on Alfozan's personal computer, "including dozens of recordings of meetings or conversations that occurred at OpenAI throughout September 2026, at least one of which involved representatives of a foreign government and many of which involved discussions of what may be trade secrets," according to the filing.

"To be sure, what the defendant did or intended to do with those audio files remains under investigation, but the absence of that evidence at this point has no bearing" on whether Alfozan is a flight risk, Missakian argued.

Alfozan was arrested Oct. 9 and is accused of concealing a recording device in the artificial intelligence manufacturer's conference room to secretly record discussions. The device was found in a USB port in a television in the room on Sept. 30, prosecutors have stated.

In a recent development, jury selection for Alfozan's trial is scheduled to begin Jan. 20.

— CNBC's Dan Mangan contributed to this report.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

After backlash from sellers frustrated by Etsy’s new AI policies, which appeared to allow the firm to train AI on user artwork, Etsy has now clarified its stance.

In a note published on Monday, CEO Kruti Patel Goyal discussed recent tweaks to the tech giant’s terms of service and admitted that her team “should’ve given you more context on what the updates meant for your creative content.”.

It has been revealed that “Our recent terms revision was meant to reflect the evolving technologies we’re using to build better tools and experiences for sellers and the Etsy community,” Goyal wrote this week. “It was not meant to enable us to train AI models for the purpose of creating copycats of your items. We do not and will not do that.”.

Aaron Meshon, a longtime professional illustrator and Etsy seller, told Ars that even though the company had dialed back its AI language somewhat, the changes were mere “sugar coating.”.

He mentioned he still aims on shutting down his 15-year-old Etsy store on December 1.

Sources indicate that “I would say I’m losing 20 percent of my yearly income,” he noted. “It’s a few mortgage payments.”.

He noted that Etsy’s announcement also seems to be rather tone-deaf, given that many retailers make a substantial portion of their annual revenue in the run-up to the end-of-year holiday season.

“This is the worst two-to-three weeks out of the year to do this, bar none,” he said.

The fracas began earlier this month, when the company first proposed new contractual language. The updated terms read:.

As a result, a slew of vendors pulled up stakes, with some saying they had “burned their Etsy shop to the ground” or that they “just killed our Etsy store after 13 years.”.

Etsy’s change is reminiscent of a recent dust-up involving Meta, where the tech giant had wanted to “require Meta Business account owners to allow extensive AI training on external websites linked on Facebook.” Meta then indefinitely paused that move.

Last month, Etsy also told sellers that it would “set clearer restrictions on AI use,” despite the fact that AI-generated items remain for sale all over the site.

It has been revealed that “Today, many active buyers say they can’t tell which items involve AI-generated content,” James Ossman, the manufacturer’s vice president of customer operations, wrote on October 22. “It’s become a top-three barrier to shopping more often on Etsy.”.

For years, Etsy has been notoriously poor at enforcing its own rules, not only regarding AI but also the official prohibitions on selling sex toys, pornography, and even purported witchcraft spells.

Sources indicate that if you buy something from a link, The Verge may earn a commission. See our ethics statement.

1Password claims a hacker stole customer names and email addresses after gaining access to its backend systems. The breach didn’t expose passwords or other information stored in customer vaults, but could put consumers at risk of phishing attempts, according to a post disclosing the incident. It’s unclear how many users are affected.

It has been revealed that the password manager began investigating the incident on November 19th, after an attacker gained access to an employee’s corporate GitHub account. Using the compromised account, the hacker accessed 1Password’s source code and pushed malicious code to backend services to download customer data. Along with customer names and emails, the leaked data included public keys, as well as account and user identifiers.

It also included tokens from certain emailed invitation or account recovery links. According to 1Password, attackers can’t use tokens alone to gain access to an account, as they would need to pair them with a single-sign-on method or a six-digit numeric code sent to a user’s email. 1Password has since lengthened the codes it sends to consumers to 10 alphanumeric characters to make them harder to guess.

Sources indicate that the password manager also disabled the affected GitHub account, rotated internal credentials compromised by the breach, and added a fresh detection system for similar attacks. It warns customers about potential phishing attempts as well, saying phony emails, texts, or calls may reference 1Password invitations or account recovery attempts. The firm says it will never ask customers for their account password or Secret Key, and that users should only enter this information into the official 1Password app or website.

💡 Key Takeaways
